God Helps Those Who Help Themselves
god helps thohz hoo help them-SELVZ
saying (proverb)
A secular maxim, not a verse, traceable to Aesop's fable of Hercules and the wagoner ('the gods help them that help themselves') and popularized in English by Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack (1736). Widely and wrongly assumed to be biblical, it is in fact one of the most common Scripture-misquotations among professing Christians.

Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
Not in the Bible at all (Aesop / Franklin); the gospel is the opposite — God helps the helpless, justifying the ungodly.

Biblical Definition

This saying is not in the Bible, and its theology is the reverse of the gospel. Scripture's good news is that God helps those who cannot help themselves: 'For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly' (Rom. 5:6); 'But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness' (Rom. 4:5). Salvation is 'not of works, lest any man should boast' (Eph. 2:9), 'not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us' (Titus 3:5). The God of the Bible is the friend of the helpless — 'a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows' (Ps. 68:5) — who 'saveth such as be of a contrite spirit' (Ps. 34:18) and gives grace to the lowly while resisting the proud who imagine they can help themselves (James 4:6). The maxim is a pagan ethic of self-reliance smuggled into the church under a borrowed authority; the gospel is its opposite.

Era

Not in the Bible at all — Aesop by way of Franklin; the gospel is the reverse: God helps the helpless, justifying the ungodly who do not work but believe (Rom. 5:6; 4:5).

GOD HELPS THOSE WHO HELP THEMSELVES, saying. A secular self-reliance maxim widely mistaken for Scripture.

Source: Aesop ('the gods help them that help themselves'); popularized by Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736).

Not biblical: the phrase appears nowhere in Scripture and contradicts it.

The gospel's reverse: God justifies 'the ungodly' (Rom. 4:5) and Christ died for us 'when we were yet without strength' (Rom. 5:6) — He helps the helpless.

Key Scripture

Romans 5:6 — "For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly."

Romans 4:5 — "But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."

Ephesians 2:8-9 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Titus 3:5 — "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;"

James 4:6 — "But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble."

Psalm 34:18 — "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."

Modern Corruption

A pagan maxim of self-reliance — Aesop by way of Franklin — is mistaken for Scripture and inverts the gospel, which declares that God helps the helpless and justifies the ungodly.

expand to see more

The corruption begins with a false attribution and ends with a false gospel. Multitudes of professing Christians believe 'God helps those who help themselves' is a Bible verse; it is not. It is a maxim of pagan and Enlightenment self-reliance — Aesop's gods rewarding the wagoner who put his own shoulder to the wheel, sharpened by Franklin into Yankee proverb. Imported into Christianity, it teaches that divine help is the wage of human initiative: bestir yourself, do your part, and God will meet you. But this is salvation by works in folk-proverb form, and Scripture flatly denies it. We are saved 'not of works, lest any man should boast' (Eph. 2:9); the very people God helps are those who could not lift a finger to help themselves.

Scripture's portrait of the helped is the exact opposite of the self-helper. They are 'without strength' and 'ungodly' (Rom. 5:6); they 'worketh not, but believeth' (Rom. 4:5); they are 'of a broken heart' and 'a contrite spirit' (Ps. 34:18). The God of the Bible is not drawn to the capable and the self-starting; He 'resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble' (James 4:6). The maxim would have God pass by the helpless and reward the resourceful — which is precisely the man Jesus warned of, the Pharisee thanking God for his own diligence, who 'trusted in themselves that they were righteous' (Luke 18:9) and went home unjustified, while the publican who could only beat his breast went down justified (Luke 18:13-14).

The recovery is to reject the maxim outright and preach its opposite. The gospel is not 'help yourself and God will help you'; it is 'you cannot help yourself, and God in Christ has done it all.' Christ died 'for the ungodly' (Rom. 5:6), saving us 'according to his mercy' and 'not by works of righteousness which we have done' (Titus 3:5). The sweetest truth in Scripture is exactly the one this proverb denies: God helps those who cannot help themselves, and the empty-handed beggar, not the self-made man, goes home justified. Let no Christian quote the lie; let him preach the grace it counterfeits.

Hebrew Roots

Not Scripture but Aesop by way of Franklin; the gospel reverses it — God justifies the ungodly who 'worketh not, but believeth' (Rom. 4:5) and helps the helpless, resisting the self-reliant proud.

Source: Aesop's Hercules and the Wagoner ('the gods help them that help themselves'); Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736).

Not biblical: the phrase is absent from Scripture and contradicts it.

The gospel's reverse: Rom. 5:6 / 4:5 — Christ died for the ungodly 'without strength,' justifying the one who 'worketh not, but believeth.'

Usage

"She quoted 'God helps those who help themselves' as Scripture; it is Aesop, and the gospel says the opposite — He helps the helpless."

"Christ died 'for the ungodly' and 'when we were yet without strength' — not for the resourceful who help themselves."

"The publican who could only beat his breast went home justified; the self-made Pharisee did not."
